\section[repente]{repente — suddenly, unexpectedly}

\label{lesson:LA-C292-repente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for not yet, then the Latin for at last.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: repente}
\textbf{repente} — \textquotedblleft{}suddenly, unexpectedly\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Repente magna pluvia cecidit, et omnēs fūgērunt.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Suddenly heavy rain fell, and everyone ran away.}
\end{quote}

The ablative of the old adjective \emph{repēns}, 'sudden'. Close to \emph{subitō} (taught), and common in Livy.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{repente} is the ablative of \emph{repēns}, \textquotedblleft{}sudden\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), used as an adverb. Where \emph{repēns} itself comes from is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[cōnfestim]{cōnfestim — at once, without delay}

\label{lesson:LA-C292-confestim}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for at last, then the Latin for suddenly.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: cōnfestim}
\textbf{cōnfestim} — \textquotedblleft{}at once, without delay\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Dux, ubi nūntium audīvit, cōnfestim mīlitēs mīsit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{When the leader heard the news, he sent soldiers at once.}
\end{quote}

Common in Caesar and Livy for a swift reaction: one thing heard, the next done.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cōnfestim} is linked by Lewis \& Short with \emph{festīnō}, \textquotedblleft{}to hurry\textquotedblright{} (taught), with the prefix \emph{con-}: all in a rush. The exact formation is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[continuō]{continuō — straightaway, without a pause}

\label{lesson:LA-C292-continuo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for suddenly, then the Latin for at once.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: continuō}
\textbf{continuō} — \textquotedblleft{}straightaway, without a pause\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Puella epistulam lēgit et continuō flēvit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The girl read the letter and straightaway burst into tears.}
\end{quote}

The adverb of \emph{continuus}, 'unbroken': nothing comes between. Do not confuse the verb \emph{continuō, continuāre}, 'to join in a row'.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{continuō} is the ablative of \emph{continuus}, \textquotedblleft{}unbroken\textquotedblright{}, which is built on \emph{contineō}, \textquotedblleft{}to hold together\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB). English \emph{continue} comes from the same family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[extemplō]{extemplō — in an instant, forthwith}

\label{lesson:LA-C292-extemplo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for at once, then the Latin for straightaway.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: extemplō}
\textbf{extemplō} — \textquotedblleft{}in an instant, forthwith\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Extemplō portae clausae sunt.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{In an instant the gates were shut.}
\end{quote}

Old and lively in tone: Plautus, Vergil and Livy use it. Plautus also has the longer \emph{extempulō}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{extemplō} comes, says Lewis \& Short, from \emph{ex} and \emph{tempulum}, a diminutive of \emph{templum} in its old sense \textquotedblleft{}a marked-out space\textquotedblright{}: out of the very moment.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[prōtinus]{prōtinus — immediately; straight on}

\label{lesson:LA-C292-protinus}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for straightaway, then the Latin for in an instant.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: prōtinus}
\textbf{prōtinus} — \textquotedblleft{}immediately; straight on\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ē raedā dēscendit et prōtinus domum festīnāvit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He got down from the carriage and hurried straight home.}
\end{quote}

First in space, 'onward, straight ahead'; then in time, 'at once'. Both senses are classical.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{prōtinus} is built on \emph{prō}, \textquotedblleft{}forward\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{tenus}, \textquotedblleft{}as far as\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): onward, and then without a break.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
